scenes.title: Picture the forces acting together

beats.text: Consider a box resting on a rough, level floor. A horizontal pull and a second, sloping pull are applied together.
Both pulls act together. The box slides right and gains speed. The sloping rope pulls forwards and upwards; the floor still supports the box.
We will check why friction cannot hold it still, and find how quickly it speeds up. Here is the whole question.

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: The box has mass four kilograms and starts at rest.
A constant horizontal pull P of nine newtons acts to the right.
A second constant force Q of eight newtons acts thirty degrees above the horizontal, also to the right.
The coefficient of friction is zero point two five. Take g as ten metres per second squared.
Contact with the rough horizontal floor is maintained. These are the only applied forces. Use the ideal friction model: while sliding, friction equals its limiting value.
Find the normal reaction and the actual friction. Decide whether the box moves, and find its acceleration. First, separate the angled force into components.

scenes.title: One angled force, two components

beats.text: The angle is measured from the horizontal. The horizontal side is adjacent; the vertical side is opposite.
The horizontal component H equals Q cosine theta.
Substitute eight and thirty degrees. H equals four root three newtons, to the right.
The vertical component V equals Q sine theta.
Eight sine thirty gives four newtons upwards.
The components replace Q. Do not count the original angled force again. H helps pull along the floor; V changes how much the floor must support.

scenes.title: Vertical balance gives the reaction

beats.text: Contact is maintained on a level floor, so vertical acceleration is zero. Reaction and the upward component support the box against its weight.
Resultant force equals mass times acceleration. Vertically, the resultant is zero.
Taking upwards positive, R plus V minus m g equals zero.
Substitute four for V, four for the mass, and ten for g.
Rearrange: reaction equals weight minus the upward component.
R equals thirty six newtons. This positive reaction confirms that floor contact is possible.
The rope provides some upward support, so the floor provides less. This is why you cannot automatically set reaction equal to weight.

scenes.title: Can friction keep the box at rest?

beats.text: At rest, friction adjusts to the horizontal demand, up to a limit. Actual friction f is less than or equal to mu R.
The maximum friction is mu times the normal reaction.
Zero point two five times thirty six gives a maximum of nine newtons.
Now find the horizontal demand D, before subtracting friction. Add the horizontal pull and the angled force’s horizontal component.
Nine plus four root three newtons. The extra positive component makes this greater than the nine newton limit.
Friction cannot balance that demand. The box starts sliding right. Only now use the sliding model: actual friction equals the maximum, nine newtons left.

scenes.title: Use the horizontal resultant to find acceleration

beats.text: Take right as positive. Both horizontal pulls act right; friction acts left. Weight and reaction have no horizontal components.
Newton’s second law: resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
The horizontal resultant is P plus H minus f, so P plus H minus f equals m a.
Substitute nine plus four root three, minus nine, equals four a.
The nines cancel. Four root three equals four a.
Divide both sides by four. The acceleration is root three metres per second squared, to the right.
With constant forces, that acceleration stays constant. Starting from rest, the box gains speed. Notice the increasing distance it travels in equal time intervals.

scenes.title: What changes if the force pushes down?

beats.text: What would change if the sloping force pushed downwards instead, at the same angle? Would the friction limit stay the same? Think about the floor’s support.
With downward component V, vertical balance becomes R minus V minus m g equals zero.
So R equals m g plus V. The floor supports both weight and the downward push. Reaction increases, and so does the friction limit.
The horizontal component stays the same. Recheck the demand against the new limit before deciding the actual friction.
